Parameterized analytical solution of seepage equation for reservoir simulation using physics-informed kolmogorov-arnold network without labels
Article preview
Abstract

abstract:
Abstract
Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a crucial role in the description of physical phenomena; however, traditional numerical methods face significant challenges regarding computational complexity and high-dimensional problems. Although Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising approach for solving PDEs, they face certain limitations in terms of generalization and computational efficiency, particularly for complex problems such as the seepage equation with source-sink terms. We propose an innovative method for solving the seepage equation with source-sink terms efficiently and accurately, without labels, without meshing, using asymptotic networks and Physically Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (AS-PIKAN), and express its parameterized analytical form with parameters. This model combines asymptotic and correction networks. The asymptotic network captures the asymptotic behavior of the equation and offers initial approximations, whereas the correction network leverages the interpretability of KAN for refinement. Ultimately, we derive a mathematical expression for the parameterized analytical solution of the seepage equation. Experimental results show that after obtaining the parameterized analytical solution, its solving speed is about 4.3 times faster than traditional numerical methods, while maintaining a solution accuracy within the range of 10–4 to 10–2.

  - heading "Introduction" [level=2]
  - generic: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are extensively utilized in science and engineering as fundamental mathematical tools for modeling diverse natural phenomena. Traditional numerical methods, such as finite difference, finite element, and boundary element methods, have achieved significant advancements in solving PDEs [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]. However, traditional numerical methods encounter significant challenges when applied to high-dimensional problems due to their substantial computational complexity and time consumption. Specifically, the impact of mesh generation and resolution on solution accuracy, the complexity of boundary condition handling, and limitations in applicability to irregular geometries pose numerous challenges in solving complex PDEs [[6], [7]]. Moreover, traditional methods often struggle to maintain accuracy and stability when addressing nonlinear and multiscale problems [[6], [7], [8], [9], [10]].
  - generic: With the advent of deep learning and neural networks [[11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17]], Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a novel solution for solving PDEs [[18], [19]]. By incorporating physical laws and PDEs into the loss function of neural networks, PINNs enable models to fit data while adhering to physical constraints [20]. This approach circumvents the complexity of traditional numerical mesh generation and is particularly suited for solving PDEs in high-dimensional spaces or complex geometries. However, PINNs still face challenges when dealing with complex dynamical systems, discontinuous solutions, and high-dimensional fractional PDEs [[21], [22], [23]]. Especially for nonlinear seepage equation with source and sink terms, existing methods often struggle to achieve stable convergence or accurately capture their multiscale and nonlinear characteristics.
  - generic: To overcome these limitations, researchers have explored improvements to the PINNs framework by redesigning the loss function. For instance, Fu et al. (2024) [24] enhanced the expressive power of model by embedding PDE information into activation functions. Wang et al. (2024) [25] introduced physical causality mechanisms to improve the accuracy of model for inverse problems. Antonio et al. (2024) [26] employed gradient annihilation strategies to enhance robustness when handling discontinuous solutions. While these methods have improved PINN performance for specific physical problems, they still fall short in fundamentally characterizing the complex dynamics of source and sink dominated nonlinear seepage problems.
  - generic: Refining prediction strategies can significantly enhance the performance of PINNs. Guo et al. (2022) [27] utilized Monte Carlo methods to refine node distributions in solving fractional PDEs. Liu et al. (2023) [28] proposed a transfer learning framework to enhance training stability. Cao et al. (2024) [29] developed an asymptotic pretraining strategy to improve the ability of model to capture rapidly changing initial and boundary conditions. Yuan et al. (2024) [30] presented a Physics-Informed Convolutional Neural Network framework based on discrete schemes, accelerating convergence through memory mechanisms. Although these innovations enhance adaptability of PINNs to complex boundary structures and initial conditions, their generalization capability and interpretability remain insufficient when dealing with seepage equation.
  - generic: Despite these advancements, challenges related to training processes and solution accuracy persist when using PINNs to solve complex PDEs. Chen et al. (2021) [31] proposed a data-free surrogate model with attention mechanisms to improve stability. To reduce model complexity, Radial basis function-based PINNs effectively handle high-frequency features and ill-conditioned computational domains while preserving local approximation properties [32]. Wu et al. (2025) [33] combined fuzzy representations with uncertainty modeling, introducing deep fuzzy PINNs to counteract the interference of sparse noisy data on solution accuracy. However, most current improvement strategies rely on fine-tuning and empirical heuristics, lacking a unified and interpretable modeling approach for nonlinear seepage behaviors.
  - generic: Although PINNs demonstrate strong capabilities in solving PDEs, they still exhibit significant limitations in expressing analytical solutions for complex PDEs. Traditional neural networks rely on fixed activation functions, weight matrices, and bias terms to establish input-output mappings [[34], [35], [36]], but this inherent mechanism faces two major challenges. First, the variability of network parameters makes the modeling process difficult to trace, resulting in low transparency and interpretability. Second, while PINNs can approximate PDE solutions with high accuracy, they fail to provide explicit analytical expressions[[37], [38], [39]]. For example, in 2023, although our proposed asymptotic solution network can solve nonlinear seepage equation, the residual network used cannot provide explicit asymptotic solutions and has the problem of low computational efficiency [39].
  - generic: To overcome these limitations, researchers have begun exploring novel network architectures grounded in mathematical theory. Among these, Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) have showed promise. In contrast, the KAN presents a novel network architecture based on the Kolmogorov and Arnold representation theorems [40]. When applied to solving PDEs, KAN utilizes learnable activation functions that not only illustrate the progressive approach of the network to PDEs solutions but also confer greater adaptability and flexibility upon the model. This approximation method enables KAN to adaptively adjust its internal functions, thereby enhancing the interpretability of the model and enabling it to represent analytical solutions of PDEs.
  - generic: Existing studies primarily conduct network architecture level comparisons, systematically evaluating the performance of MLPs and various KAN structures in solving PDEs. These works focus on how choices of basis functions, regularization strategies, and training techniques influence the convergence behavior and expressive capacity of the models. In addition, some studies investigate the integration of KAN into different PINN frameworks highlighting how KAN can enhance the training stability and solution accuracy of PINN-based methods [[41], [42]].
  - generic: "The seepage equation with source and sink terms exhibits complex nonlinear characteristics, making its analytical solution challenging to obtain. This paper presents a method for solving the seepage equation without labels, based on an asymptotic network and Physics-Informed KAN (AS-PIKAN), which represent the analytical solutions of these equations. The AS-PIKAN model primarily comprises two components: an asymptotic network and a correction network. The asymptotic network is constructed based on the asymptotic solution forms of the single-phase seepage equation, capturing its asymptotic behavior to provide an initial approximation of the solution. The correction network is designed based on KAN, utilizing its interpretability to refine the analytical solution provided by the asymptotic network and describe the corrected solution mathematically. By integrating the asymptotic network and the correction network, the AS-PIKAN model not only maintains high precision in solutions but also significantly enhances computational speed, enabling the construction of analytical solution forms. This method offers a novel and effective approach for solving the unlabeled solutions to the seepage equation."
  - generic: "The second section of this paper provides foundational knowledge by introducing the single-phase seepage equation, its asymptotic solutions, and the KAN framework. The third section outlines the AS-PIKAN method for deriving analytical solutions to the single-phase seepage equation, including the construction of the loss function, model architecture, algorithm, flowchart, and representation of the analytical solutions. The fourth part is a set of experiments using AS-PIKAN to solve the seepage equation, categorized into two types: homogeneous and heterogeneous reservoirs. This section includes experimental setups, solution comparisons, error analysis, evaluations of computational speed, and comparative experiments."
